inline.s: [SECOND, one must not keep the mind in wait for enlightenment. Because our wonderfully perfect, genuine mind is originally without duality. In the past, because of the condensation of delusive thought, mind and objects, faculties and dusts, stand opposed to one another, and therefore one gives rise to delusion and creates karma. Now, for a cultivator there is just a single thought. Let go of body, mind, and the world, and simply hold up this one thought and press forward; do not care whether it is enlightenment or no enlightenment — only keep going, thought after thought, step after step. If the work reaches the point, one will naturally see his original face; why be in a hurry to plan ahead? If one keeps the mind in wait for enlightenment, this very waiting-mind is the root and trunk of birth and death. One may wait until the eons are exhausted and still never awaken, because one has not understood the truly undual mind, and thinks there is something else besides it. If the waiting-mind is not removed, weariness easily arises, and one for the most part falls back. It is like seeking a thing and not finding it, and then giving rise to the thought of stopping and resting.]

Second, do not keep the mind in wait for enlightenment. Because our wonderfully perfect, genuine mind is originally without duality. In the past, because of the condensation of delusive thought, mind and objects, faculties and dusts, stand opposed to one another, and therefore one gives rise to delusion and creates karma. Now, in cultivation one does the work on a single thought. Let go of body, mind, and the world; simply hold up this one thought (mind-contemplation or Chan investigation) and press forward. Do not care whether it is enlightenment or not — only keep doing it, thought after thought, step after step. If the work reaches the point, one will naturally see his original face; why make plans in advance? If one keeps the mind in wait for enlightenment, this very waiting-mind is the root of birth and death. Waiting until the Year of the Donkey and the Month of the Horse, one still cannot awaken. This is because he does not understand the truly undual mind, and thinks there is something else besides it. If the waiting-mind is not removed, weariness easily arises, and one for the most part falls back. It is like seeking a thing and not finding it, and then giving rise to the thought of stopping and resting.

[Without duality (juedai)] To be free of all opposing pairs. Opposing pairs means the mutual opposition of two sides, such as black and white, large and small, good and evil, and so on. Without duality is the equality of thusness, in which no Dharma is obtained, and so it is free of all opposing pairs; for short it is called juedai (without duality). It is synonymous with the absolute.

[THIRD, one must not long for the wonderful fruit. Because the delusive mind of birth and death of sentient beings is originally the fruit-body of the Tathāgata. Now, sunk in delusion, [one] transforms the spiritual powers and wonderful functions of the Buddhas into delusive thoughts and feelings and discriminating views; transforms the true and pure Dharma-body into the substance of the karma of birth and death; transforms the pure and wonderful land into the realms of the six dusts. Now, doing the work, if in a single thought one suddenly awakens to his own mind, it is like the great forge, casting and fusing the myriad forms. This very body, mind, and world are originally the fruit-body of the Tathāgata; these very delusive thoughts and feelings are originally the spiritual powers and wonderful functions; only the names are changed, not the substance. Yongjia says: “The real nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the empty body of illusion is the Dharma-body.” If one can awaken to this Dharma-gate, then the feelings of taking and rejecting are forgotten, the mind of delight and disgust is stilled: every step is the Avataṃsaka Pure Land, and every thought is Maitreya's descent into birth [to become a Buddha]. If one first settles the mind seeking the wonderful fruit, this mind of longing is the root of birth and death, and obstructs right knowledge and vision. The more one seeks, the further away one goes; when the strength of seeking is exhausted, weariness arises.]

Third, do not long for the wonderful fruit. Because the delusive mind of birth and death of sentient beings is originally the fruit-body of the Tathāgata. (When self-nature is deluded, it is a sentient being; when self-nature is awakened, it is a Buddha.) Now, with self-nature sunk in delusion, [one] transforms the spiritual powers and wonderful functions of the Buddhas into delusive thoughts and feelings and discriminating views; transforms the true and pure Dharma-body into the substance of the karma of birth and death; transforms the pure and wonderful land into the realms of the six dusts. Now, in doing the work, if in a single thought one suddenly awakens to his own mind, it is like the great red furnace of that which creates and transforms, casting and fusing the myriad forms. This very body, mind, and world are originally the fruit-body of the Tathāgata; these very delusive thoughts and feelings are originally the spiritual powers and wonderful functions; only the names are changed, not the substance. As Master Yongjia says in the Song of Realizing the Way: “The real nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the empty body of illusion is the Dharma-body.” If one can awaken to this Dharma-gate, then the feelings of taking and rejecting are forgotten, the mind of delight and disgust is stilled: every step is the Avataṃsaka Pure Land, and every thought is Maitreya's descent into birth (becoming a Buddha). If one first settles the mind seeking the wonderful fruit, this mind of longing is the root of birth and death, and obstructs right knowledge and vision. The more one seeks the wonderful fruit, the further away one is from realizing the Way; seeking without obtaining, one's strength is exhausted, and weariness arises.
[The great smelter (daye)] A metaphor for that which creates and transforms [creation].

[FOURTH, one must not give rise to doubt oneself. Whenever doing the work, [one should] all along let go of body and mind, and shut off seeing, hearing, perception, and knowing. Having left the old steps behind, looking forward is dim
(in ancient usage the same as “dim and distant”)

and obscure, with no place to settle body and mind. Advancing, there is no new realization; retreating, one loses the old home. If one calculates and worries about front and back, then a doubting mind arises. One gives rise to countless reckonings, weighing gain and loss. Or one engenders arbitrary opinions apart from this, stirring up perverse thoughts, obstructing right knowledge and vision. This must be broken through, and then one proceeds straight in with determination, no longer harboring hesitation. Generally, when the work reaches the point where one can no longer do it, that is precisely where the strength lies; with even greater spirit, one will not retreat or shrink back. Otherwise, one falls into the demon of sorrow.]

Fourth, do not give rise to doubt oneself. Whenever doing the work, once one lets go of body and mind and shuts off seeing, hearing, perception, and knowing, and has left the familiar old road behind, looking forward on the new road it is again strange and boundless, with no place to settle body and mind. Advancing, there is no new realization; retreating, one loses the old home. In such a situation, if one calculates and worries about front and back, then a doubting mind arises. Thereupon one gives rise to countless reckonings, weighing gain and loss. Or one engenders subjective views apart from this, stirring up perverse thoughts, obstructing right knowledge and vision. This point must be broken through, and then one proceeds straight in with determination, no longer harboring hesitation. Generally, when the work reaches the point where one can no longer do it, that is precisely where the strength lies; one should rouse one's spirit further and continue, and then one will not retreat or shrink back. Otherwise, one falls into the demon of sorrow.
[Spirit (jingcai)] Vigor; energy.

[FIFTH, one must not give rise to a mind of terror. This means that when the power of thought in the work is urgent and pressing, [if] the delusive thoughts suddenly stop for a single thought, and suddenly body and mind drop away into emptiness, one then sees the great earth with not an inch of soil, deep beyond the infinite, and a great terror arises. If one does not break through this, one dares not go forward. Or one takes this expansive emptiness as something superb and wondrous. If one grasps this emptiness, then a great perverse view arises, denying cause and effect — this is the most dangerous point.]

Fifth, do not give rise to a mind of terror. When the power of thought in the work is urgent and pressing, and the delusive thoughts suddenly stop for a single thought, and suddenly body and mind drop away into emptiness, one then sees the great earth with not an inch of soil, deep beyond the infinite, and a great terror arises. If one does not break through such a state, one dares not go forward. Or one takes this expansive emptiness (everything empty) as a superb and wondrous state. If one grasps this emptiness as a superb and wondrous state, then a great perverse view arises, and one no longer believes in cause and effect — this is the most dangerous pass.
[Denying cause and effect (bowu yinguo)] Negating cause and effect. “Bo” means to cast away. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “Denying cause and effect, going entirely into emptiness.”

[SIXTH, be firmly resolved to believe that your own mind is Buddha. Yet there is no other Buddha besides this; the mind itself is it. Because the Buddha's true Dharma-body is like empty space. If one realizes that delusion is originally empty, then the originally present Dharma-body reveals itself of itself, bright and still, perfect and all-pervading, without lack and without excess. Do not again let the mind run outward in pursuit; if one abandons this mind and seeks elsewhere, then in the mind there arise all sorts of countless dream realms. These are precisely the manifestations of the consciousness-spirit; one must absolutely not regard them as anything extraordinary. Yet, in my pure and clear mind, there is originally no thing, and not even a single thought. Whenever one gives rise to a thought and sets the mind moving, that already violates the substance of the Dharma.]

Sixth, be firmly resolved to believe that your own mind is Buddha. Yet there is no other Buddha besides this; the mind itself is it. Because the Buddha's true Dharma-body is like empty space. If one realizes that delusions are originally false, then the originally present Dharma-body reveals itself of itself, bright and still, perfect and all-pervading, without lack and without excess. Do not again let the mind run outward in pursuit; if one abandons this mind and seeks elsewhere besides it, then in the mind there arise all sorts of countless dream realms. These are precisely the illusory manifestations of the consciousness-spirit; one must absolutely not regard them as anything extraordinary. You should know that in my pure and clear mind there is originally no thing, and not even a single thought. Whenever one gives rise to a thought and sets the mind moving, that already departs from the substance of the Dharma.

[SEVENTH, one must know that delusive thoughts are originally false. Those doing the work now generally do not know that the delusive thoughts of their own mind are originally false. They take these delusive thoughts to be real, and only make an adversary of them. This is like a child playing with the shadow of a lamp: the more one plays with it the less relations one has with it, and playing long enough one comes to be frightened by it. There is another kind, who fear delusive thoughts and wish they could seize them and cast them aside. This is like grasping at the wind and catching at shadows; all day long one wrestles with them, using up all one's strength, and never for a single thought is there respite. Entangled for so long, one's faith day by day grows weary. One then says that Chan practice has no efficacy, and gives rise to a mind of slander, or a mind of terror, or a mind of retreat — this is a common ailment of beginners. There is no other reason for it than that one has not understood that the abiding true mind is of a nature neither arising nor ceasing, and only takes delusive thoughts to be real Dharmas. Here one must absolutely pass through; if one would pass through this barrier, there is naturally an upward-road beyond.]

Seventh, one must know that delusive thoughts are originally false. Those doing the work now generally do not know that the delusive thoughts of their own mind are originally false. They take these delusive thoughts to be real, and only make an adversary of them. This is like a child playing with the shadow of a lamp: the more one plays with it the less relations one has with it, and playing long enough one becomes frightened by the shadow of the lamp itself. (This is to say: if one takes delusive thoughts to be real and makes an adversary of them, it is like a child playing with the shadow of himself on a wall — not only do the delusive thoughts fail to cease, but the more one plays the stranger it becomes, and after a long while it seems like a devil, and one is frightened.) There are another kind, who fear delusive thoughts and wish they could seize them and cast them aside. This is like grasping at the wind and catching at shadows; all day long one rolls about with them, using up all one's strength, and never for a single thought is there respite. Entangled for so long, one's faith day by day grows weary. One then says that Chan practice has no efficacy, and gives rise to a mind of slander, or a mind of terror, or a mind of retreat — this is a common ailment of those beginning to learn. There is no other reason for it than that one has not understood that the abiding true mind is of a nature neither arising nor ceasing, and only takes delusive thoughts to be real Dharmas. Here one must absolutely pass through; if one can pass this barrier, there is naturally an upward-road beyond.

[EIGHTH, one has only to investigate apart from mind and consciousness and seek apart from the realm of delusive thoughts. As soon as a thought arises, whether good or evil, set it aside on the spot; absolutely do not make an adversary of it. Truly believe that in your own mind there is originally no such thing. Just take up the huatou [you are] investigating and lift it with effort, like the vajra sword, striking down both demons and Buddhas. Here one most needs great courage, great vigor, and great endurance. One absolutely must not calculate front and back, and absolutely must not be timid and weak. Only with a straight mind and right thought, bracing oneself and going forward, will one naturally stand lofty and imposing, not entangled by these delusive thoughts, like a hawk that has slipped free of the leather armguard. Through all the hours of the day and night, amid all circumstances and conditions, one is naturally not obstructed and fettered, naturally attaining great ease and great freedom — this is the point where the beginner gains strength in the first step of the work.]

Eighth, one has only to investigate apart from mind and consciousness and seek apart from the realm of delusive thoughts. As soon as a thought arises, whether it be good or evil, set it aside on the spot; absolutely do not make an adversary of it. Truly believe that in your own mind there is originally no such thing. Just take up the huatou [you are] investigating and lift it with effort, like the vajra sword — when a demon (an evil thought) comes, cut down the demon; when a Buddha (a good thought) comes, cut down the Buddha. Here one most needs great courage, great vigor, and great endurance. One absolutely must not calculate front and back, and absolutely must not be timid and hesitant. Only with a straight mind and right thought, bracing oneself and going forward, will one naturally stand lofty and imposing, not entangled by these delusive thoughts, like a hawk that has slipped free of the leather armguard, freely soaring. Through all the hours of the day and night, amid all circumstances and conditions, one is naturally not obstructed and fettered, naturally attaining great ease and great freedom — this is the point where the beginner gains strength in the first step of the work.

[Mind (xin), intention (yi), and consciousness (shi)] Mind refers to the eighth consciousness (the ālayavijñāna), intention refers to the seventh consciousness (the manas), and consciousness refers to the remaining six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness). [A hawk that has slipped free of the armguard (tuo gou zhi ying)] Like a hawk whose leg strap is released and that escapes the leather armguard — a metaphor for no longer being constrained; gou
gōu
was a leather armguard worn when shooting arrows in ancient times.

[The several points above are much like drawing legs on a snake — they are but provisional words for the occasion. They are not the ultimate, nor are they real Dharmas. It is because, being on the road, fearing that at the first step out the door one may fall into the divergent bypaths, wasting effort of mind and vainly losing time, [I have spoken them]. One must truly take the one gate that exits onto the sublime and wonderful path of adornment. What is called walking evenly and uprightly, swift as the wind: in one's course one can multiply a day into a kalpa. In short, the upward-road of the Buddhas and patriarchs does not involve a journey's length; yet for the beginner's expedient means, one must also pass through from here.]

The several points I have spoken above are much like drawing legs on a snake — they are but provisional words for the occasion. They are not the ultimate, nor are they real Dharmas. Because you have already set out on the road, fearing only that you might err at this first step out the door, stray into a wrong path, waste effort of mind, and vainly lose time, I have reluctantly spoken these words. In cultivation one must take a true path to Buddhahood (the sublime and wonderful path of adornment that exits through the one gate). If the path is right and the method also right (walking evenly and uprightly, swift as the wind), then the swiftness of advance is like what would require a whole kalpa to attain, now attained in a single day. In short, the upward-road of the Buddhas and patriarchs does not require going so great a distance or spending so long a time to realize the fruit. Even at the first step of a beginner, one must understand this principle.

[The one gate that exits onto the sublime and wonderful path of adornment (yimen chaochu miao zhuangyan lu)] The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “At that time the World-Honored One, in the midst of the assembly, stretched out his golden arm and stroked Ānanda's head, and instructed Ānanda and the great assembly: There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha's Crown Heroic Śūraṅgama King, endowed with all practices; by this one gate the Tathāgatas of the ten directions exit onto the sublime and wonderful path of adornment.” The full title of the Śūraṅgama Sutra is “The Sutra of the Great Buddha's Crown, the Tathāgata's secret cause, the ultimate meaning of cultivation and realization, the myriad practices of all bodhisattvas, the Heroic Śūraṅgama.” [The Heroic Śūraṅgama (shou lengyan)] The name of the samādhi attained by the Buddha. [Course (xinglü)] Walking. [The upward-road of the Buddhas and patriarchs does not involve a journey's length] The Essentials of Mind Transmission says: “Yet there is quickness and slowness in realizing this mind. There are those who, upon hearing the Dharma, in a single thought attain the mind of no-mind; there are those who attain the mind of no-mind only upon reaching the ten stages of faith, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications; there are those who attain the mind of no-mind only upon reaching the ten grounds. Whether long or short, only when one attains the mind of no-mind is one settled; there is then nothing more to be cultivated or realized. In truth there is nothing attained — this is genuinely not false. One who attains in a single thought and one who attains on the tenth ground have exactly the same function, with no greater or lesser depth; it is merely that through many eons one has vainly undergone toil.”
